I am sure members on both sides, cabinet ministers of today and yesteryear included, will realize how little one knows about a subject when one is brought to decide upon it. What government members admit, and what cabinet ministers will tell you, is that party discipline is there. They feel that because they are the government the Lord has anointed them for the next four or five years, that they have all knowledge and that they can do no wrong. We know that is not so.
What I am asking of those members who sat through all the committee hearings this summer on the Bank Act and of other members who sat in 1978-79 during the public hearings and who worked on the committee report, those who saw a great number of changes, is that they read my amendment very carefully. Subsection (1) imposes a degree of silence; the Inspector shall not disclose to any other person except the minister, the deputy minister of finance, the governor of the Bank of Canada, a representative of the deputy minister of finance or of the governor of the Bank of Canada, if authorized in writing, or directors of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, any information regarding the business or affairs
of a bank or its customers. Similarly, confidentiality is imposed with respect to information:
(b)	received in the course of an international exchange of information contemplated by paragraph (2)(b)\ or
(c)	furnished to the Inspector pursuant to subsection 303(7)
These are particular returns which are given to the Inspector General of Banks and I say in my amendment that notwithstanding this the inspector shall disclose on a confidential basis, to any standing or special committee of Parliament. That imposes a responsibility upon the members of any standing or special committee of Parliament charged with the examination of the business of banking-and I use that phrase because I think I know what it means, having tried to put it in the act. This is another reason why hon. members should vote for my amendment later tonight or tomorrow. My amendment says:
-the Bank Act, or any statutes of Parliament relating thereto, information
(a)	regarding the business or affairs of any bank carrying on business in Canada
I do not say "of its customers". Notice that.
Over in section 251(1 )(<a) the information that is to be kept secret is information concerning the business or affairs of a bank 1 do not think members need to know anything about the affairs of the customers, so it is deliberately left out of my amendment. But a different position is rather if it is regarding the business affairs of any bank or is:
(b)	received in the course of an international exchange of information such as is referred to in paragraph (2)(b)
(c)	furnished to the Inspector pursuant to subsection 303(7)
(d)	of a general nature pertaining to the business of banking
These are position papers within the Department of Finance or which the Inspector General of Banks may have, provided such information is requested of the inspector in a formal resolution adopted by such a committee. This is not merely somebody teeing off and saying, "Oh, I would like to know something about what happened to that particular bank". It is in keeping with the degree of knowledge of which members of a banking committee should be apprised.

bers so that members may serve on one or two committees and there is not the massive change and platooning to keep up strength because of fear that there might be a vote. speechtext: You are absolutely right.

speechtext:
Once a committee begins work, its membership should remain and when a member comes on, let him pick up the testimony of the past and read. The good Lord gave him the ability to read. To come to committee absolutely green on a subject and, as 1 say, reinvent the wheel, is not the way in which a committee should be conducted.
In any event, how does one obtain this information when the committee decides, two or three years down the road, that, for instance, it would like some information, about reciprocity? Remember, the Inspector General cannot be summoned on the examination of estimates. How much time can the finance committee spend on the examination of estimates when it is already overloaded? What we require is a careful preparation of the information requested by the committee, and then the committee may debate that information. I hope it is not a case where one side sits there with a hedgehog mentality to protect the government's interests. All members are responsible for the passage and for intelligent consideration of legislation, and I would like to see an improvement in our work. I suggest that such a proposal should be implemented in many other fields. 1 hesitate to suggest income tax because we would never get around to studying all the questions, but there are many other fields of legislation, I think, in which this amendment could apply with equal facility. speechtext:
Motion No. 50
That Bill C-6, an act to revise the Bank Act, to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act and the Bank of Canada Act, to establish the Canadian Payments Association and to amend other acts in consequence thereof, be amended in clause 2 by striking out line 29 at page 308 and substituting the following therefor:
"ten per cent of the total domestic assets"
He said: For the edification of certain members who felt 1 was wrong on my last stand and perhaps for the edification of the minister who came in contact with this act only this year, 1 want to point out that motion No. 50 is designed to restore to the legislation a conclusion which the banking committee reached in March, 1979. It was composed of senior members on the then government side along with others from this side.
The whole question had been very carefully considered with witnesses and public testimony, and had been discussed with the Inspector General of Banks. It was decided that the volume of business to be ultimately allowed for foreign banks within ten years, bearing in mind the degree of inflation that might be around, could go up to 10 per cent of the total domestic assets of Canadian banks. The original white paper had said 8 per cent of the assets contained in schedule Q, quite a different formula. I remember the then member from Montreal, Mr. Jacques Trudel-I see his successor-had been successful in negotiating on the government side and that was for 10 per cent. That was a more appropriate figure. Lo and behold, somebody in the Department of Finance or the Inspector General of Banks put it at 8 per cent. No one has ever told us why. There have been no reasons other than it was a judgment decision.
In putting forward this amendment, 1 want to question the inability to obtain the information as to why it was done, and to establish that bureaucratic decisions shall not prevail over decisions of House committees. We are charged with determining the policy and the legislation. I find it, frankly, a
supine attitude to accept, if we accept it, that the bureaucracy should tell a House committee or this House what policy should be.
I have put down this motion to discuss that point and to emphasize it. I do not like that situation. If hon. members will reflect upon it, I think they will agree with me. This happens all too often, particularly in legisation of this kind. There was public testimony. The committee worked hard and came to a conclusion. As is often the case, there was some negotiation. Then some faceless individual in the background made a change. They told me that the cabinet approved. Even on this side, I can tell you how cabinet approves. The bill slides through and that feature does not get drawn to the attention of the cabinet committee or of the whole cabinet in approving the legislation.
I know what happened at the time the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was minister of finance and a bill was okayed to go through with the figure changed. I do not know who changed it, but it was changed to some figure judged more important by a bureaucrat. That has to stop. If a House committee decides as a matter of policy that there shall be a certain level of activity by foreign banks as compared with Canadian banks, it is not up to any bureaucrat to downgrade that figure.
The minister cannot tell me why it is at 8 per cent. He has not been told. He was not responsible for that, except in the technical sense that he has been charged with bringing the legislation forward in this House and must assume responsibility for it. However, the point I want to make is that he does not know.
When dealing with my previous motion, the minister said he thought we already had sufficient information. The minister should blush a little, because the motion now before us points to a situation in which he knows the committee did not have the information it should have been given. We should have much more information. The previous committee set the figure at ten. The minister in this legislation says it is eight. No reasons have been given for the change.
Long before this minister ever came near the legislation, somebody had written in the figure eight. Why? That is something that we, as legislators, should know. It is a situation over which we have no control. We do not have the control over legislation that we should have in Parliament. That is a regrettable lesson I have learned over many years.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-TRANSLATORS' DISPUTE-STATE OF NEGOTIATIONS
PUBLIC SERVICE-TRANSLATORS' DISPUTE-STATE OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7 I put a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) which was answered by his parliamentary secretary. It dealt with the alleged refusal of Treasury Board officials to permit the Department of the Secretary of State to predetermine the amounts of the salary deductions which would apply during the slowdown period. Of course I was referring to the strike of the translators. On the preceding Monday, November 3, an agreement was reached on the essential points. As a matter of fact, on the day in question I gave the President of the Treasury Board my understanding of the agreement which the translators were prepared to accept. Essentially it was the agreement which was eventually signed.
However, from that Monday until the following Friday, there was continuing conflict on one point. It was that the translators who had admittedly been on a "go-slow" campaign for some weeks in the summertime were to be penalized. A deduction would be made from their salaries, and they wanted some idea of either the amount to be deducted or the basis upon which the deduction was to be calculated.
The problem we are running into is one we have encountered in many instances in negotiations. It came up again in a release of the Public Service Alliance of Canada dated November 12 protesting the threat of what they term "unwarranted disciplinary action". In this second case it was again the threat of a deduction from salary or non-payment of salary should certain employees who ordinarily provided services in both official languages choose to speak only one language. In the second case, involving the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, the employees are not paid a bilingualism bonus and that is their particular problem. The difficulty, Mr. Speaker, stems from the fact that in both cases there is a classification difficulty and, as we know, classification is not bargainable.
1 have brought up the subject many times in the past five years. It was almost five years ago-in fact in February next we will be celebrating the fifth anniversary-that a report was tabled in this House popularly known as the Finkelman committee or, more properly, the Joint House of Commons and Senate Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service. That committee tabled 72 recommendations to improve the bargaining situation and morale in the public service. No action has been taken on any of those 72 recommendations and I suggest we are finding ourselves in difficulty today because no action has been taken. Although we have the excuse of the elections having taken place and changing governments, we cannot get away from the fact that five years later we still have these problems recurring on almost a monthly basis.
1 am not going to pronounce on whether classification should be bargainable or not. In fact, that was not one of the recommendations although it was suggested that it be discussed by the parties. In both cases-in the translator's strike and the problem with the second group of the Public Service Alliance of Canada-part of the difficulty stems from separating the normal requests of a bargaining group from this issue of classification which, according to existing legislation, is not bargainable.
Mr. Speaker, the issue still remains. The strike of the translators was settled but I repeat my request to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) and to whichever hon. gentleman is speaking for him tonight: when are we to get some answer from the President of Treasury Board on actions he proposes, either in the way of acceptance or refusal, with regard to the 72 recommendations to improve working conditions and morale in the public service which were tabled in this House in February almost five years ago?

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-TRANSLATORS' DISPUTE-STATE OF NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government commends the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert) for his initiative this evening in raising this question.
As was announced by the Treasury Board on November 10, 1980, a settlement has been reached with the Canadian Union of Professional and Technical Employees representing the translation group, subject to ratification by the union members. This agreement was reached with the assistance of Mr. Maurice Cantin, Acting Chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, following earlier mediation attempts by Mr. Ken Strike.
The agreement incorporated recommendations made by Mr. Strike and, as has been announced, included an understanding concerning actions taken during the strike by the Department of the Secretary of State to dock the pay of employees who were at work but who did not perform their work in accord-
November 17, 1980

ance with departmental directives or standards. This agreement provides that in certain instances the over-all number of person days for which the department had determined that payment should not be made would be limited to 1,000 and recognizes the principle that pay should be directly related to satisfactory performance of the work. This understanding does not apply to disciplinary actions taken by the department for unlawful actions committed during the strike. In such cases, employees can, of course, resort to the normal grievance procedure. Further consultation on a number of these matters is taking place between the department and the union.
The Treasury Board is nearing the conclusion of a review of employer-employee relations in the public service. The hon. member is very familiar with the various important events which have taken place in the review of employer-employee relations in the public service over the past several years. This review, of course, commenced with Mr. Jacob Finkelman's report which was received in March, 1974. As the hon. member is fully aware, the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service of Canada reported to Parliament in 1976. Earlier, in 1975, as a result of preliminary recommendations of that committee, amendments to the Public Service Staff Relations Act were enacted, principally providing for a full-time Public Service Staff Relations Board. I should note that while Mr. Finkelman recommended a series of changes in the Public Staff Relations Act, he found that the basic structure of the legislation was sound. In its report, the Special Joint Committee recommended the establishment of a special task force to review the Public Service Employment Act and the role of the Public Service Commission in personnel management and employer-employee relations in the public service.
Together with that recommendation, as the hon. member will recall, the committee recommended that the review include an examination of the role assigned to the Public Service Commission and its relationship with Treasury Board and the Public Service Staff Relations Board. In response to this recommendation, the government in 1977 established the Special Committee on the Review of Personnel Management and the Merit Principle, which produced what is known as the D'Avignon report. The report of his committee was received in September, 1979.
It should also be noted that during this same period, the Royal Commission on Financial Management and Accountability had been established. Its report was published in March, 1979. As the President of the Treasury Board noted in his reply to questions posed by the hon. member before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates on November 3, 1980, Mr. W. A. B. Anderson has the responsibility, under his direction, for co-ordinating the government's response to both the Lambert report and the D'Avignon report.
As the President of the Treasury Board noted at that time, it is his intention to bring forward a complete response to the
Adjournment Debate
recommendations of these two reports. As mentioned earlier, the Treasury Board is in the process of completing a review of employer-employee relations in the public service, including the recommendations of the Finkelman report, the report of the special joint committee and certain pertinent recommendations of the D'Avignon report and the Lambert report. It is anticipated that this review will be completed in the not-too-distant future and that it will be followed by the introduction of any necessary amendments to the appropriate legislation.
In conclusion, I note that the President of the Treasury Board, in replying to the hon. member's last question before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, indicated that he "has made some very constructive suggestions in the past" and hoped he would continue to do so in the future.

VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE AND DISABILITY PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 4, 1980, as reported at page 4400 and 4401 of Hansard, I asked the acting Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lamontagne) the following questions:
The minister must be aware of the fact that recipients of war veterans allowance have been particularly hard hit by the cruel and devastating budget brought down by the Minister of Finance, in contrast to measures proposed by this party which would have protected these veterans. Will the minister recommend to cabinet that the war veterans allowance and disability pensions be increased, in view of the fact that any benefit from the veterans affairs will passed in July has now been wiped out?
My supplementary question was:
I should like to ask the acting minister if the government will incorporate in the Pension Act on a permanent basis a formula to keep the basic rate of disability pension adjusted to increases in the pay scales of the five selected categories of public service workers in order to offset the harmful effects of this harsh budget?
As Conservative spokesman for veterans affairs, I feel it is my duty to get some straight answers out of the government as to how it intends to cushion the devastating effect of this budget on veterans with low and fixed incomes. The Crosbie budget had built in an energy tax credit which would have resulted in a rebate of $200 a year for a family of four, or $80 per individual taxpayer. I have been receiving letters from pensioners and widows. Typical of these letters is the one 1 received from London, Ontario, dated November 10. It reads:
I read in our paper that the government is going to give $21 million to improve veterans health care. That's nice, but what are they going to do for us poor veterans widows? They gave us a $10 raise recently. It should have been $100 more per month so we could at least be equal to a senior citizen. We are all living far below the government poverty line, so we should at least be brought up to that level. Don't you agree?
I certainly agree. I would also like to point out that OAP recipients who receive the guaranteed income supplement and live at home have now fallen 22 per cent below the poverty line.
Unless there is a substantial increase in the basic rate of disability pensions and a parallel increase in WVA rates, veterans will be falling very far below the poverty line. We were most pleased to see the minister's announcement of the program for aging veterans last week. We have long supported
4788	COMMONS DEBATES	November 17, 1980
Adjournment Debate
the idea of veterans being able to maintain themselves in their own homes where possible, and we welcome this step. However, this offers assistance to only a very small percentage of veterans. We must work to help the neglected categories. Very few veterans can afford to run a car these days. In some cases, however, a small car provides transportation to and from medical appointments plus limited city driving. With gas up as much as 40 cents a gallon, some of these veterans will have to take their cars off the road. To add insult to injury, some Liberal members are stating in their "Householders" that by the end of this year, gasoline will have gone up 13.3 cents per gallon though we know the figure should be 40 cents a gallon. That is a cruel hoax on every Canadian citizen.
It is estimated that the basic rate of disability pension will fall $500 behind the basic rate for the five selected categories of public servants by 1981. This is just not good enough. The government must act now to tie the basic rate to the five categories. Our veterans should not have to go cap in hand year after year asking for an increase. They should have the same security as the civil servants and the ability to plan ahead for their needs.
In presenting a motion in this House on November 4, my hon. friend from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) stated the following:
Whereas more than 10,000 widows of deceased veterans and some 9,000 of their children were promised pension benefits over the next six years under Bill C-40, whereas many of these widows are left below the poverty line and may not survive until 1986 or 1987 and since the care of veterans and their widows and children is a national obligation and not just another piece of social legislation, I move-
That this House request the government to find the money this year to pay these widows and children their proper pension benefits.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will have some good news for us.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE AND DISABILITY PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in responding to the hon. member's question, I would state that I have just returned from a visit to France and Belgium where I visited the graves of our fallen comrades. 1 would like to point out that our benefits in Canada are superior to those in other countries.
I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) for an opportunity to provide the House with information concerning the positive action taken by this government to help Canada's veterans and their families.
In July 1980 a bill which made very significant improvements to veterans legislation received royal assent. Contrary to the implication contained in the hon. member's, question, all war veterans allowance recipients will continue to have their allowances increased quarterly in keeping with any increases in the consumer price index. In addition, the allowances of those under 65 years of age were increased by $10 per month
for single recipients and $12 per month for married recipients effective July 1, 1980.
Furthermore, similar increases will be automatically awarded annually until by April 1, 1986, the allowance levels for recipients over and under 65 years of age will be identical. Bill C-40 also provided that all future increases in either OAS or GIS rates will automatically be incorporated in the same amounts in WVA and CWA.
Over the next six and a half years some $150 million will go to veterans because of these measures and because of this government's promise to help those persons who need it most.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN WAR VETERANS ALLOWANCE AND DISABILITY PENSIONS
speechtext:
On January 1, 1981 the basic rate of disability pensions is being increased by 9.7 per cent in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index. This means that the amount payable to an unmarried disability pensioner whose disability is assessed at 100 per cent will be increased to $811 a month or $9,737 a year. Married 100 per cent pensioners with two dependents will receive $1,196 a month or $14,629 per year. All other pensions and allowances will be increased in the same proportion.
The Government of Canada remains committed to helping veterans and their families. We are always looking for ways to improve veterans' legislation to meet changing needs of veterans. To answer my hon. friend's interjection at the moment widows are presently receiving pensions at the 47 per cent to 38 per cent rate, and next April 1 widows of pensioners who were receiving pensions of between 48 per cent and 33 per cent will be eligible for these benefits. Those disabled veterans I was able to see during my visit to those countries are certainly entitled to it. Members of the Legion, two presidents of councils, have agreed that the proposals put forward by the late minister, the Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald, are to their benefit.
